lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.text: Good morning, Lakeside Hotel. How can I help you?

lines.speaker: Caller
lines.text: Oh, hello. I'd like to book a room for three nights, please.

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.text: Certainly. Which dates were you thinking of?

lines.speaker: Caller
lines.text: The fourteenth, fifteenth and sixteenth of March.

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.text: Let me check. Yes, we have rooms available then. Would you like a single or a double room?

lines.speaker: Caller
lines.text: A double room, please. And do you have any rooms with a sea view?

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.text: We do, but they're slightly more expensive. A standard double is eighty-five pounds per night, and a sea-view double is one hundred and ten.

lines.speaker: Caller
lines.text: I'll go for the sea view. It's a special occasion.

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.text: Lovely. Can I take your name, please?

lines.speaker: Caller
lines.text: It's Margaret Sullivan. That's S-U-L-L-I-V-A-N.

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.text: Thank you, Ms Sullivan. And a contact phone number?

lines.speaker: Caller
lines.text: Sure, it's oh-seven-four-one-two, five-three-six, nine-eight-seven.

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.text: Great. Will you be arriving by car?

lines.speaker: Caller
lines.text: Yes, I will. Is there parking at the hotel?

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.text: There is, and it's free for guests. Just register your number plate at reception when you check in.

lines.speaker: Caller
lines.text: Perfect. What time is check-in?

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.text: Rooms are available from two p.m. Check-out is by eleven a.m. on your final day.

lines.speaker: Caller
lines.text: That's fine. Could I also book breakfast?

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.text: Of course. Breakfast is served from seven until ten, and it's twelve pounds per person if you book in advance.

lines.speaker: Caller
lines.text: Yes, please include breakfast for both of us.

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.text: Noted. So, a sea-view double room for three nights, with breakfast for two, arriving on the fourteenth of March. Is that all?

lines.speaker: Caller
lines.text: One more thing — do you have Wi-Fi in the rooms?

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.text: Yes, Wi-Fi is free throughout the hotel. The password is 'lakeside'.

lines.speaker: Caller
lines.text: Excellent. That's everything. Thank you very much.

lines.speaker: Guide
lines.text: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to the City Museum. My name's David, and I'll be your guide today. The tour will take about an hour, and we'll finish back here at the main entrance.

lines.speaker: Guide
lines.text: Before we set off, let me point out a few important things. The main entrance, where you're standing now, is here at the bottom of your map, marked A. The information desk is just inside, on your right, and that's where you can collect audio guides for five pounds.

lines.speaker: Guide
lines.text: Now, if you look at your map, the café is directly to the left of the entrance. It's a good spot to rest, and it closes at four thirty.

lines.speaker: Guide
lines.text: Moving further inside, the main exhibition hall is in the centre of the museum. It currently houses a special exhibition on ancient Egypt, which has been extended until the end of August because it's so popular.

lines.speaker: Guide
lines.text: To the east of the exhibition hall is the natural history gallery. It was recently refurbished, and it's one of the most popular sections with children, mainly because of the dinosaur skeletons.

lines.speaker: Guide
lines.text: On the west side of the hall, you'll find the art gallery. Please note that photography is not allowed in this part of the museum.

lines.speaker: Guide
lines.text: Finally, the gift shop and toilets are in the north-east corner, next to the exit. The gift shop offers a ten percent discount to members.

lines.speaker: Guide
lines.text: Right, if everyone's ready, we'll begin our walk towards the exhibition hall.

lines.speaker: Tutor
lines.text: Right, so let's hear how your research project is going. Maria, would you like to start?

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.text: Sure. We're looking at how students use the university library, and whether the new online catalogue has changed their habits.

lines.speaker: Tutor
lines.text: And what have you found so far?

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.text: Well, we did a survey of about two hundred students, and the results were quite surprising. We expected most students to prefer online resources, but actually a lot of them said they still like studying in the library itself, mainly because it's quiet.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Yes, and when we asked about the online catalogue, many students said they use it to find books, but then they borrow the physical copies rather than reading e-books.

lines.speaker: Tutor
lines.text: That's interesting. What about the group study rooms?

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.text: Those are very popular. Students said they're often fully booked, especially during exam periods. We think the library should add more rooms.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: We also found that opening hours are a problem. The library closes at ten, but many students want it to stay open until midnight, especially postgraduate students.

lines.speaker: Tutor
lines.text: And how are you planning to present this?

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.text: We're going to produce a report with charts showing the survey results, and we'll give a short presentation to the library committee next month.

lines.speaker: Tutor
lines.text: That sounds sensible. Make sure you include some direct quotes from students — they make the report more persuasive.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Good idea. We'll do that.

lines.speaker: Tutor
lines.text: One more thing — have you thought about the limitations of your study?

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.text: Yes, we know the survey only covered one week, so it might not reflect the whole year. We'll mention that in the report.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: Good morning. Today I'd like to talk about urban heat islands — a phenomenon that affects nearly every large city in the world.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: An urban heat island occurs when a city is significantly warmer than the surrounding countryside. The difference can be as much as five or six degrees Celsius on a calm summer night. This may not sound dramatic, but it has real consequences: higher energy use for air conditioning, greater strain on power grids, and increased health risks during heatwaves.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: So why do cities get so hot? There are several reasons. First, dark surfaces. Asphalt roads and dark rooftops absorb sunlight and store heat, then release it slowly after sunset. In contrast, rural areas with vegetation reflect more sunlight and cool down quickly through evaporation.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: Second, cities lack vegetation. Trees and plants cool the air through a process called evapotranspiration, in which water evaporates from leaves and takes heat with it. When a city replaces parks with concrete, it loses this natural cooling.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: Third, waste heat from human activity. Cars, air conditioners and factories all release heat directly into the urban environment.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: Fortunately, there are solutions. One of the most effective is planting more trees and creating green roofs — roofs covered with vegetation that absorb less heat and provide insulation. Another approach is using light-coloured materials for roads and buildings, which reflect sunlight instead of absorbing it. Some cities have also introduced 'cool roofs', which are coated with reflective paint.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: Research suggests that a combination of these measures could reduce urban temperatures by several degrees, making cities more comfortable and more resilient as the climate warms. The challenge, of course, is funding and political will — but as heatwaves become more frequent, the case for action grows stronger every year.
